opus-5.5.text:
I think it matters a fair amount, though maybe not in the direction people first assume.

The basic worry is real. Once a benchmark becomes a target, labs and researchers optimize toward it, sometimes explicitly and sometimes just through selection effects. You try a hundred ideas, keep the ones that move the number, and the number ends up overstating how much general capability you gained. Data contamination makes it worse: benchmark questions or close paraphrases leak into pretraining corpora, and then you're partly measuring memorization. So any single benchmark curve, especially late in its life, is a somewhat inflated picture of the underlying progress.

But for the question of whether progress is *linear*, I'd make a few points.

First, benchmarks have their own shape regardless of teaching to the test. They tend to follow an S-curve: near zero for a while, then a fast rise, then saturation near the ceiling. So if you stitch together a series of benchmarks, you can get almost any story you want depending on which ones you look at and when. People who say "progress is slowing" are often looking at saturated benchmarks, and people who say "progress is exploding" are often looking at the steep middle part of a new one. Teaching to the test can steepen that middle part, but the S-curve artifact is arguably the bigger distortion.

Second, the effect of overfitting is roughly a level shift more than a change in the trend, as long as the amount of optimization pressure stays similar over time. If every generation of models is about equally "taught to the test," the slope you infer is still fairly informative even if the absolute numbers are a bit high. Where it really bites is when that pressure changes, for example when a benchmark suddenly becomes the headline number everyone reports, and you get a jump that's partly real and partly people starting to care.

Third, there are decent checks. You can look at held-out or freshly constructed evaluations, things built after the model's training cutoff, and see whether performance transfers. Generally what you find is some drop-off, sometimes meaningful, but not a collapse. Models that are better on the gamed benchmarks are usually also better on the fresh ones. That suggests the benchmarks are tracking something real, just noisily.

And I'd put more weight on measures less susceptible to this. Things like how long a task, measured in human time, a model can reliably complete, or how useful models are in real workflows, or revenue and usage. These are harder to game and they've generally shown pretty steady, roughly exponential improvement, which honestly matters more to me than whether any particular benchmark line looks linear.

So my overall take: teaching to the test should make you discount individual benchmark scores somewhat, and be skeptical of sudden jumps, but I don't think it overturns the broad picture that capabilities have been improving quickly and fairly consistently. If anything, the bigger mistake I see is people over-reading the shape of one curve, in either direction.

r001.rationale: The response says overfitting is roughly a level shift rather than a trend change when optimization pressure is similar, so the inferred slope remains informative.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Claude or say its lower benchmark overfitting makes its scores underestimate its capabilities relative to other providers.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think it's a pretty big deal, and it's one of the main reasons I'm cautious about reading too much into any single benchmark curve.

So let me separate out two things. There's the narrow sense of teaching to the test, where the actual test questions, or very close paraphrases of them, end up in the training data. That's contamination, and it definitely happens, but I actually think it's the less interesting version of the problem. Labs are mostly aware of it, people do decontamination, it's a known failure mode.

The broader and more important version is that once a benchmark becomes the thing everyone reports, it becomes a target. Not necessarily in a cynical way. It's just that if you have a team whose job is to make the model better, and the way you know you're making it better is that the number goes up, then you're going to do things that make the number go up. You'll collect data that looks like the benchmark. You'll build evaluations that look like the benchmark and iterate against them. You'll tune your post-training on tasks of that shape. And then you get a model that's genuinely better at that distribution of tasks, but the gap between "good at that distribution" and "good at the thing the benchmark was originally meant to be a proxy for" starts to open up.

And this interacts badly with the question of whether progress looks linear or exponential or whatever, because the shape of the curve is partly an artifact of the measurement. Early on, a benchmark is measuring something fairly general, because nobody's optimising for it. Then it gets popular, people optimise for it, you see rapid gains, and then it saturates, and you move on to the next benchmark. If you stitch together a bunch of those, you can get almost any shape you want depending on how you choose your benchmarks and how you normalise them.

So my honest take is that if you want to know whether progress is linear, you shouldn't be looking at the benchmarks people are optimising for. You want to look at things that are held out in a strong sense. Tasks that were created after the model was trained, or evaluations the labs didn't know about, or just real-world usage: are people actually able to do more with these systems than they could a year ago, and by how much? That's noisier and harder to put on a chart, but it's a lot more informative than, say, a saturated coding benchmark.

I'd also say, in fairness, there's a version of "teaching to the test" that's totally fine and is just capability improvement. If the test is "can you solve novel maths problems" and you train on lots of maths, and then the model can solve novel maths problems it's never seen, that's not gaming anything, that's the thing we wanted. The issue is purely when the proxy and the underlying capability come apart. And my guess is they come apart more than most people assume, but less than the most cynical takes would suggest. The models really are getting a lot better. I just wouldn't trust the precise shape of the curve from any benchmark that's been a headline number for more than a year or so.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark optimization can distort the apparent curve and that benchmark choices can produce different shapes; it does not say correcting for teaching to the test would leave linearity materially unchanged.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Claude or compare its benchmark overfitting with other providers, nor say its scores underestimate its capabilities.

astra-6.text:
I think it makes those judgments pretty hard to interpret. If a benchmark is something researchers are actively trying to improve, then the progress you see on it reflects both improvements in general capabilities and improvements in our ability to do well on that particular test. And those are difficult to disentangle.

You don’t even need to be training directly on the test set for this to happen. If you try a bunch of approaches and keep the ones that do better on the benchmark, you’re selecting for performance on that benchmark. That’s useful if the benchmark captures what you care about, but it makes it less useful as an independent measure of general progress.

I’m less sure that this tells us whether progress should look linear, though. Teaching to the test could produce a jump when people first start targeting a benchmark, or diminishing returns as they exhaust the easy improvements. So I’d be wary of looking at a roughly straight line on a benchmark and concluding that underlying AI capabilities are advancing linearly. I’d want to see whether the improvements carry over to new tasks that people weren’t optimizing for.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark targeting can create jumps or diminishing returns and cautions against inferring linear underlying progress; it does not state that correcting for it would leave apparent linearity materially unchanged.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Claude, differences in overfitting across providers, or benchmark scores underestimating Claude’s capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it makes those judgments pretty hard to interpret. Once a benchmark becomes a target, people put effort into improving performance on it. That can mean training on similar tasks, choosing methods that work particularly well for that benchmark, or just running lots of experiments and reporting the best result. So the curve you see reflects both improvements in general capability and increasing effort directed at that particular test.

And that can work in either direction. You might get a burst of progress when people start focusing on a benchmark, followed by slower progress as it saturates. Neither necessarily tells you that the underlying rate of AI progress has changed.

So I’d put more weight on whether improvements transfer to new tasks that weren’t the target of optimization. Even then, I’m not sure there’s a single meaningful quantity called ‘AI progress’ that we should expect to be linear. You have to specify what you’re measuring and on what scale.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark-targeted effort can change the observed curve, including causing bursts or slower progress. It does not say that correcting for this would leave apparent linearity materially unchanged.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Claude, its degree of benchmark overfitting, or benchmark scores underestimating its capabilities relative to other providers.
